questions.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y={e}^{x},\,x>0
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)={e}^{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y) & =x\cdot {e}^{x} \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =x{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx) & =x{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=1
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\cdot y=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{1}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\cdot y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{2}y={x}^{3}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{3}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-1/2)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-x/2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x/2}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{2}y) & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3} \\ {e}^{-x/2}\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x/2}\cdot y & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y{e}^{-x/2}) & ={e}^{-x/2}\cdot {x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}+xy={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,x>0
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y) & =x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ x\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(yx) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
x\frac{dy}{dx}+xy={x}^{2}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+y=x.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}+y) & ={e}^{x}\cdot x \\ {e}^{x}\frac{dy}{dx}+{e}^{x}y & ={e}^{x}\cdot x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y{e}^{x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot x\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{3})\,dx & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & ={e}^{x}+C \\ y & =\frac{{e}^{x}+C}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6{e}^{2x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is already in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-3$ and $Q(x)=6{e}^{2x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -3\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-3x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y) & ={e}^{-3x}\cdot 6{e}^{2x} \\ {e}^{-3x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{e}^{-3x}\cdot y & =6{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-3x}) & =6{e}^{-x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x & =\int 6{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-3x} & =-6{e}^{-x}+C \\ y & =-6{e}^{2x}+C{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and $v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{2} & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =x(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-3x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y) & ={e}^{-3x}\cdot x{e}^{3x} \\ {e}^{-3x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{e}^{-3x}\cdot y & =x\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{5}{x}y=7,\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below:

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{5}{x}$ and $Q(x)=7.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (5/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{5\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5})} \\  & ={x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{5}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{5}{x}y) & ={x}^{5}\cdot 7 \\ {x}^{5}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5{x}^{4}y & =7{x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{5})\,dx & =\int 7{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{5} & =\frac{7{x}^{6}}{6}+C \\ y & =\frac{7x}{6}+\frac{C}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x},\,x>0,\,y(\frac{\pi }{2})=1
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}y) & =x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ yx & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(\frac{\pi }{2})=1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C}{(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\ 1 & =\frac{2C}{\pi } \\ C & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{\pi }{2})}{x} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x} \\  & =\frac{\pi -2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=2x{e}^{-x},\,y(0)=-2
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=2x{e}^{-x}.$ 

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 1\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y) & ={e}^{x}\cdot 2x{e}^{-x} \\ {e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{x}y & =2x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x}) & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{x})\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{x} & ={x}^{2}+C \\ y & =({x}^{2}+C){e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =({0}^{2}+C){e}^{-0} \\ -2 & =(0+C)\cdot 1 \\ C & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=({x}^{2}-2){e}^{-x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=4{x}^{2},\,y(1)=2
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The first step is to write the equation in standard form,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)\,.
$$

In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y & =4{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x}(x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot 4{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\cdot y & =4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot 4x \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & ={x}^{4}+C \\ y & ={x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={1}^{2}+\frac{C}{{1}^{2}} \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={x}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=4$ and $Q(x)=8.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 4\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{4x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{4x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y) & ={e}^{4x}\cdot 8 \\ {e}^{4x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4{e}^{4x}\cdot y & =8{e}^{4x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{4x}) & =8{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{4x})\text{d}x & =\int 8{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{4x} & =8(\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x})+C \\ y{e}^{4x} & =2{e}^{4x}+C \\ y & =2+C{e}^{-4x}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =2+C{e}^{-4(0)} \\ -1 & =2+C(1) \\ C & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2-3{e}^{-4x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2y}{x}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}},\,y(\pi )=0
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}.$ 

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\cdot y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(\pi )=0$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+C}{{\pi }^{2}} \\ 0 & =\frac{C}{{\pi }^{2}} \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + 2y = 2e^{-2x}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y I(x) \right) = I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = 2$ and $Q(x) = 2e^{-2x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = e^{2x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x} \\ {e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2{e}^{2x}\cdot y & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y I(x)\right){:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{2x}) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac {3} {x} y = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}, \qquad x \gt 0.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = \dfrac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = x^3$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3}) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int uv'\,\textrm d x = uv - \int u' v\,\textrm d x
$$

Let $u = x, u' = 1, v' = \cos x,$ and $v = \sin x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Solve the following initial value problem using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + 3x^2y = 9x^2, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x),
$$

with $P(x) = 3x^2$ and $Q(x) = 9x^2.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x) = e^{x^3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot 9{x}^{2} \\ {e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot y & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}}) & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u = x^3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}})\text{d}x & =\int 9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =\int 3{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{{x}^{3}}+C \\ y & =3+C{e}^{-{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0) = 1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3+C{e}^{-{0}^{3}} \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y = 3 - 2e^{-x^3}.
$$
